newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish finance minister defends strong zloty.
newsitem.headline: Polish finance minister defends strong zloty.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko defended a strong zloty policy on Wednesday, saying that the growing trade deficit was no reason for weakening the currency beyond the 1997 budget's limits of 9.1 percent.
Kolodko said that the trade deficit, estimated at more than $8 billion last year, compared with $1.9 billion in 1995, should not cause concern because the current account deficit was much lower.

"After the first 11 months the current account deficit was about $1 billion, which is entirely acceptable, and in fact is a sign of health," Kolodko told parliament during the debate on the 1997 budget.

Some politicians and exporters lobbies have demanded a one-off zloty devaluation or a faster crawling devaluation of the zloty against a basket of currencies, after the imports growth rate much surpassed that of exports.

Kolodko said that considering the year-on-year producer prices growth, forecast at 10.6 percent in December 1997, and the 9.1 percent annual crawling devaluation, the zloty appreciation would be marginal and should not hit exporters.
"All exporters will find a place for themselves with no problems, if they are competitive and watch their costs," Kolodko said.
He said the imports growth was so high last year, partly because direct foreign investment, which amounted to nearly $5 billion, triggered additional purchases from abroad.
"It is estimated that each billion dollars invested directly entails additional imports of $400 million," he said.
Substantial imports last year were offset, as in previous years, mainly by robust cross-border trade inflows, Kolodko added.
